introduction.text: NextDNS is a hosted DNS filtering and security service presented by its vendor as 'The new firewall for the modern Internet' (nextdns.io, consulted 2026-11-09) [ÉDITEUR tagline]. The official site states the service 'protects you from all kinds of security threats, blocks ads and trackers on websites and in apps and provides a safe and supervised Internet for kids — on all devices and on all networks'. It is operated by NextDNS Inc., described in the vendor's own privacy policy as 'an independent company 100% funded, owned and controlled by its founders'. NextDNS is a network service, not a browser extension or application software, although client apps exist for several platforms.

what_is_it.text: A recursive DNS resolution service with per-user configuration, combining four documented function groups (nextdns.io, consulted 2026-11-09): (1) security — '10+ different types of protections' including threat-intelligence feeds of malicious domains, Google Safe Browsing, cryptojacking, DNS rebinding, IDN homographs, typosquatting, Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs), Newly Registered Domains (NRDs), parked domains, TLD controls, and CSAM blocking, with on-the-fly analysis of 'DNS questions and answers' to detect malicious behaviour; (2) privacy — ad/tracker blocklists ('millions of domains all updated in real-time'), Native Tracking Protection for OS-level trackers, and detection of 'third-party trackers disguising themselves as first-party to circumvent browsers' privacy protections like ITP'; (3) parental control — adult-content blocking, enforced SafeSearch, YouTube Restricted Mode, per-app blocking (named examples include Facebook, TikTok, Snapchat, Tinder, Fortnite), and Recreation Time schedules; (4) analytics and logs — per-device query visibility with user-controlled retention. Additional documented features: unlimited configurations, custom deny/allow lists, a customisable block page, DNS rewrites, DNSSEC validation, and experimental Handshake support.

origin_and_history.text: The founding date of NextDNS Inc. is [NON ÉTABLI] from the consulted sources. The official homepage ('Trusted by' section, consulted 2026-11-09) cites Mozilla's announcement 'Firefox Announces New Partner in Delivering Private and Secure DNS Services to Users' (blog.mozilla.org, dated 2019-12-17 in the cited URL/title) as a partnership credential — the Mozilla page itself was not consulted here, so the partnership is recorded as the vendor's citation [ÉDITEUR]. The homepage also presents testimonial quotes from named users (Leo Laporte; Vinicius Fortuna, described as 'Engineering Lead at Google's Jigsaw'; Paul Stamatiou, described as 'Designer at Twitter') [ÉDITEUR]. No corporate timeline beyond the above is established here.

operation_and_infrastructure.text: The homepage displays operational statistics [ÉDITEUR, all unverified here]: '100,000,000,000 queries each month', '15,000,000,000 queries blocked each month', and '132 server locations'; it describes an 'Ultra-Low Latency Network' with points of presence 'embedded within carriers' networks in major metropolitan areas — minimizing hops and delivering unbeatably low latency at the edge' (example latency figure 'atl 15 ms' shown). Threat detection is described as real-time: query/answer analysis 'in a matter of nanoseconds' and threat-intelligence designed to catch domains 'usually only a few hours between domain registration and the start of an attack' (vendor claims). The service works at the DNS layer: the homepage emphasises 'Zero impact on your CPU, memory or battery life — it's all done at the DNS level, not on your device'. Independent infrastructure audits or benchmarks are [NON ÉTABLI].

protocols_and_encryption.text: The official site documents encrypted-DNS support: 'Enjoy the privacy and security benefits of DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-TLS — the modern and encrypted DNS protocols' (nextdns.io, consulted 2026-11-09). DNSSEC validation is included ('Automatically validate the authenticity of DNS answers'), and the service offers 'Handshake' — 'the experimental peer-to-peer root naming system' — as an opt-in experiment [FAIT as documented feature, experimental status explicit]. Privacy-protocol engineering claims include an 'innovative in-house implementation of EDNS Client Subnet that does not expose your IP address to authoritative DNS servers' and enforced Query Name Minimisation (privacy policy). Concrete configuration endpoints (e.g. a `dns.nextdns.io`-style hostname) are [NON ÉTABLI] here: the vendor's /setup page returned an error page (HTTP 404) on 2026-11-09 (documented in the phase sources).

privacy_and_security_model.text: The privacy policy (nextdns.io/privacy, consulted 2026-11-09) makes four numbered commitments [ÉDITEUR]: (1) 'We do not (and will never) sell, license, sublicense or share any of the data submitted directly or indirectly by our users'; (2) when data 'shall not be logged, it is discarded as quickly as possible' — the server discards request/response data immediately after replying; (3) 'If not specifically requested by the user, no data is logged' — features needing retention give users 'the option, control, and full access to what is logged and for how long', under a 'What You See Is What We Have' (WYSIWWH) policy of see/export/delete; (4) protection of user privacy toward upstream interactions (privacy-preserving ECS, QNAME minimisation). Logging is therefore opt-in: retention can be set 'from one hour up to two years — or disable logging completely for a no-logs experience', and log storage jurisdiction is selectable — 'United States, European Union, United Kingdom or Switzerland' (homepage). Declared GDPR-style processors: Stripe, PayPal, BitPay (payments) and SendGrid (transactional email). Independent audits of these commitments are [NON ÉTABLI] from the consulted sources.

configuration_and_access.text: Configuration is done in a web dashboard at my.nextdns.io: the homepage offers 'Try it now' with 'No signup required' to start and 'Sign up later to save your settings'. Documented management features (nextdns.io, consulted 2026-11-09): 'Unlimited Configurations' (multiple configs per account with distinct settings), custom denylist/allowlist ('an unlimited amount of domains'), a customizable block page, DNS rewrites ('set or override the DNS response for any domain'), and per-device analytics ('See what's happening on your devices with in-depth analytics and real-time logs'). Setup is claimed 'natively supported on all major platforms — it only takes a few seconds to set up', across 'all networks — at home, on cellular, at work and on public Wi-Fi', using DoH/DoT. Commercial terms (free tier limits, paid plans) are [NON ÉTABLI] from the consulted pages; the site presents the service as free to try without specifying a pricing table.

governance_and_operator.text: The operator is NextDNS Inc. The privacy policy states the company is 'an independent company 100% funded, owned and controlled by its founders and will never engage in any data sharing or selling activities' [ÉDITEUR commitment]. Legal form, incorporation jurisdiction, team size, and funding history are [NON ÉTABLI] from the consulted sources. Data-governance posture is unusually explicit for the sector: user-selectable log jurisdictions (US/EU/UK/CH), the WYSIWWH transparency policy, and a published processor list (Stripe, PayPal, BitPay, SendGrid). Dispute/legal contact specifics beyond the privacy policy text are not established here.

limitations_and_scope.text: Limits established or observed from the consulted sources: (1) protection operates at the DNS layer — blocking is per-domain and cannot inspect non-DNS traffic (the site's own framing: 'it's all done at the DNS level'); (2) logging-dependent features (analytics, logs, Tracker Insights) require user-enabled retention — the no-logs mode forfeits them by design; (3) key evidence is vendor-published: statistics (100 B queries/month, 132 locations), protection efficacy and latency claims are [ÉDITEUR], and no independent audit appears in the consulted pages [NON ÉTABLI]; (4) configuration endpoints could not be confirmed here (setup page error) — users must obtain them from the live dashboard; (5) content-filtering blocklists are third-party/community lists ('the most popular ads & trackers blocklists'), so blocking accuracy is inherited from those lists; (6) commercial terms and free-tier caps are [NON ÉTABLI] here; (7) DNS-based blocking of apps using hardcoded resolvers or encrypted client-eDNS is outside the documented model.

advantages.text: Documented strengths: granular, user-controlled privacy — retention from one hour to two years or fully disabled, with choice of storage jurisdiction (US/EU/UK/CH) and WYSIWWH export/delete rights; unusually strong written commitments (no sale/sharing of user data; immediate discard of non-logged data; privacy-preserving ECS and QNAME minimisation); rich security layering (10+ protection categories including DGA/NRD/typosquatting/IDN-homograph detections beyond simple blocklists); per-device analytics and real-time logs; unlimited separate configurations for different networks/devices; encrypted transports (DoH/DoT) and DNSSEC; rewrites and custom block page; DNS-level operation with zero device-resource cost (vendor claim); no-sign-up trial with save-later onboarding; a cited Mozilla/Firefox partnership credential (2019).

disadvantages.text: Documented or observed limits: the no-logs mode trades away the analytics/insights features that distinguish the service; efficacy and scale claims (threat catch times, latency, query volumes) are vendor-published and not independently verified here [ÉDITEUR]; concrete setup endpoints were not confirmable from the consulted pages (setup page error on 2026-11-09); blocklist-driven filtering inherits third-party list quality (false positives/negatives possible); DNS-layer scope cannot protect against non-DNS exfiltration or enforce beyond domain resolution; commercial limits (free tier caps, paid feature gating) are [NON ÉTABLI] from the consulted pages; as a hosted service it requires trusting the operator's implementation of its policy — no independent audit is cited in the sources consulted.

who_is_it_for.text: Users who want configurable, DNS-level protection across all devices and networks with explicit privacy control: privacy-conscious users wanting opt-in logging with jurisdiction choice and delete rights; households needing parental controls (SafeSearch, YouTube Restricted Mode, app/game schedules); technical users wanting per-network configurations, rewrites and deny/allow lists (the site itself is compared by testimonial to 'Pi-hole on the cloud' [ÉDITEUR quote]); people on the move needing the same policy on cellular, work and public Wi-Fi; users wanting modern encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) plus DNSSEC with security layers beyond plain ad-blocking.

who_is_it_not_for.text: Not aimed at: users unwilling to rely on vendor-published privacy commitments without independent audits ([NON ÉTABLI] here); users needing permanent zero-log operation who also want query analytics (mutually exclusive by design); users who must confirm setup endpoints from documentation alone before starting (the consulted setup page was unusable); organisations needing contractual SLAs or enterprise support terms ([NON ÉTABLI] here); users wanting device-level content inspection rather than DNS-layer blocking; users preferring open-source self-hosted resolvers (the service is proprietary and hosted — the testimonial comparison 'cloud-hosted Pi-hole' [ÉDITEUR] highlights the contrast); users requiring non-listed storage jurisdictions beyond US/EU/UK/CH.

verdict.text: NextDNS is a hosted, configurable DNS firewall (NextDNS Inc.) combining threat-intelligence blocking, ad/tracker list filtering, parental controls and opt-in analytics over DoH/DoT with DNSSEC. Its distinguishing documented features are fine-grained logging control (retention 1 h–2 years or none; storage in US/EU/UK/CH; WYSIWWH access/deletion), explicit no-sale/no-share commitments with privacy-preserving ECS and QNAME minimisation, and multi-configuration management from a web dashboard with no-sign-up trial. Its documented limits are the DNS-layer scope, the analytics/no-logs trade-off, and the vendor-sourced nature of its scale and efficacy claims (statistics and protection claims are [ÉDITEUR]; independent audits [NON ÉTABLI]); setup endpoints were not confirmable from the consulted pages (setup page error, 2026-11-09). All cited URLs (homepage, privacy policy) were reachable; founding date and commercial terms are [NON ÉTABLI] here.
